title: Learning pronunciation
hookLine: careful teaching of how to read each word of Gurbani

lines: A GRANDMOTHER, A BOOK, A BOY.
A NOD, AND ONE WORD ALONG.
cards: On a low stool, with a small prayer book open on her knee, a grandmother faces a small boy. She reads one word. He reads it back.
She shakes her head, just slightly, and reads it again, a little slower, her finger under the letters. He tries again. This time she nods, and moves her finger one word along.
A whole afternoon can go like that, and neither of them seems to mind. Yesterday's school is known for careful reading. Today we sit in on the lesson itself.

teach.b: The word is santhiaa: teaching the correct reading of Gurbani, word by word, from teacher to student. It isn't a lecture; it's call and answer.
The teacher reads, the student repeats, the teacher corrects, the student repeats again. Why so slow? Three reasons.
First, the page. In the form installed in gurdwaras, the words of the Guru Granth Sahib run together, with no spaces between them. This is called larivar.

teach.h: LARIVAR: WHERE DOES THE WORD END?
teach.b: So santhiaa teaches where each word begins and ends, because a break in the wrong place can turn one word into two and change the meaning.

Second, the sound: how each word is spoken, vowel by vowel, so the line sounds the way the teacher received it. Third, the music. The hymns are set in ragas, to be sung, and a word placed right sits right in the tune.
The Gurus keep this care in balance. In the Var in Raag Asa, Guru Nanak has a striking salok.
In paraphrase: you may read and read, load up carts with books, fill whole caravans, fill pits and cellars, and read for a lifetime, with every breath.

teach.h: CARTS OF BOOKS: ONLY ONE THING COUNTS.
teach.b: Only one thing counts in the account; all the rest is the chatter of ego.
So santhiaa is not reading for its own sake. It's tuning the instrument. In the tradition's own picture, a correctly sounded line is a clearer door into the Name.
The grandmother and the boy aren't polishing words; they're making sure the door opens all the way.

how: Sikhs learn santhiaa from a teacher, at home, in gurdwara classes or at schools like the Damdami Taksal: the teacher reads each word of Gurbani, the student repeats it, and corrections continue until the reading is right.

o: a silent reading of the Granth done alone

games.q: you're reading a line of Gurbani written larivar, words running together, and you aren't sure where one word ends. what does santhiaa teach you to do?
o: ask the teacher, then repeat after them until it's right.
games.why: santhiaa is call and answer: the teacher reads, the student repeats, and the reading is corrected word by word.

practice: Take the word Waheguru and say it silently as a teacher would for a student, slowly: Wa, he, gu, ru. Then answer as the student, one syllable to a breath, and let them join again into one word on a single out-breath.

wordCard.voice: Santhiaa. Careful teaching of how to read each word of Gurbani: teacher reads, student repeats, until the line is sounded right. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: sound it right. Care with the sound is care with the meaning. Until tomorrow.
